Should we add atorvastatin to irbesartan for improving renoprotective effects in 
early diabetic nephropathy? A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials

Abstract 
Angiotensin II receptor blocker has exhibited their renal protective benefits in diabetic 
nephropathy. This meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effects of adding atorvastatin to irbesartan 
in early diabetic nephropathy. A systematic literature search was performed in PubMed, Embase, 
Cochrane Library, CNKI, VIP, and Wanfang database until March 25, 2019. Randomized 
controlled trials evaluating the effects of adding atorvastatin to irbesartan in early diabetic 
nephropathy were eligible. Primary endpoint was urinary albumin excretion rate, serum creatinine, 
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT


 
3
and blood urea nitrogen. Serum level of total cholesterol, triglyceride, fasting blood glucose, 
interleukin-6,and C-reactive protein (CRP) as well as blood pressure were secondary endpoints. 
Seventeen trials involving 1,390 patients were identified. Compared with irbesartan alone, 
co-administration of atorvastatin and irbesartan significantly reduced urinary albumin excretion 
rate (weighted mean differences [WMD] -21.22 μg/min; 95% confidence interval [CI] -26.95 to 
-15.50), serum creatinine (WMD -6.46 μmol/L; 95%CI -8.52 to 4.39),BUN (WMD -0.46 mmol/L; 
95%CI -0.64 to -0.27), total cholesterol (WMD -1.79 mmol/L; 95%CI -2.34 to -1.23), triglyceride 
(WMD -0.93 mmol/L; 95%CI -1.20 to -0.67),and systolic blood pressure (WMD -2.27 mmHg; 
95%CI -4.01 to -0.53), CRP (standard mean difference [SMD] 1.57; 95%CI -2.24 to -0.9), and 
Interleukin-6 (SMD 1.53; 95%CI -2.29 to -0.78). However, there was a significantly increased risk 
of nausea/vomiting (risk ratio 3.15; 95% CI 1.18–8.38) on the co-administration group. In 
conclusion, adding atorvastatin to irbesartan achieves additional renal protective benefits in early 
diabetic nephropathy patients. However, these findings should be interpreted with caution due to 
suboptimal methodological quality of the analyzed trials. 
 
Keywords: atorvastatin; irbesartan; diabetic nephropathy; randomized controlled trials; 
meta-analysis.  
 
1. Introduction 
Diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease are both major public health challenge. Diabetic 
nephropathy is a common consequence of long-standing diabetes mellitus. Approximately 
30–40% of type 2 diabetic patients have progressed to renal impairment [1,2]. In China, the 
estimated number of patients with diabetic nephropathy was 24.3 million [3]. Despite strict 
glycemic and hypertensive control, about 20% diabetic patients will eventually develop end-stage 
renal diseases [4]. Current therapeutic strategies for diabetic nephropathy are mainly focused on 
the blood pressure and glycemic control [5]. However, these approaches did not completely delay 
the progression of diabetic nephropathy [6]. Therefore, seeking novel therapies to prevent the 
progression of diabetic nephropathy remain an unmet need. 
  
Various factors including hyperglycemia, albuminuria, hypertension, and dyslipdemia are 
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT


 
4
associated with progression of diabetic nephropathy [7]. Hyperlipidemia is currently recognized as 
a major determinant of progression of renal disease in diabetes [8]. Statins have attracted much 
attention in diabetic nephropathy. A well-designed meta-analysis has summarized that statins 
could reduce the albuminuria and urinary albumin excretion rates in type 2 diabetic patients with 
nephropathy [9]. Antihypertensive recommendations have been existed for diabetic nephropathy. 
Either angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) 
monotherapy was associated with slowed nephropathy progression in diabetic patients [10]. Since 
the approval of ARB therapy for the treatment of diabetic nephropathy in patients with type 2 
diabetes, there has not been a new medication approved by the US FDA for the therapy of diabetic 
nephropathy [11]. In addition, despite several RCT showed a dramatic benefit with ARB therapy, 
many patients on this therapy still had renal events[12-14]. 
 
A number of clinical trials have examined the add-on effect of atorvastatin to irbesartan for 
patients with diabetic nephropathy [15-23]. However, most of these trials were limited by small 
sample sizes or single center designs. No previous meta-analysis has been performed to assess the 
effect of adding atorvastatin to irbesartan on the progression of diabetic nephropathy. To answer 
whether should add atorvastatin to irbesartan for treatment of early diabetic nephropathy, we 
conducted this meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to evaluate the potential 
additional benefits of atorvastatin in these patients. 
 
2. Methods 
2.1.Search strategy  
This meta-analysis was reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for 
Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) statement [24]. A systematic literature search 
was performed in PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, CNKI, VIP, and Wanfang database until 
March 25, 2019. Relevant trials were identified by the following search terms and medical subject 
headings: “atorvastatin” AND “irbesartan” AND “nephropathy” OR “kidney disease OR “renal 
disease” AND “diabetic” OR “diabetes” AND randomized controlled trials OR random. 
References of relevant articles were manually searched for additional potentially relevant trials. 
2.2. Study selection 
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT


 
5
Trials satisfying the following inclusion criteria were included: 1) RCT design; 2) enrollment 
of patients with early diabetic nephropathy defined as urinary albumin excretion rate (UAER) 20 
to 200 μg/min [25]; 3) comparison of atorvastatin plus irbesartan and irbesartan alone; and 4) 
primary endpoint was 24-h urinary protein excretion. Serum level of creatinine, blood urea 
nitrogen (BUN), total cholesterol (TC), triglyceride (TG), fasting blood glucose (FBG), 
interleukin-6, C-reactive protein (CRP), blood pressure, and adverse events were secondary 
endpoints. Trials were excluded if: 1) different regimens applied between two treatment groups 
apart from atorvastatin; 2) not reporting the stage of diabetic nephropathy; and 3) retrospective 
studies or duplicated publication. 
2.3. Data extraction and quality assessment 
Two authors independently extracted the following data: first author’s surname, publication 
year, trial design, sample sizes, age, baseline UAER, serum level of creatinine, BUN, TC, TG, 
FBG, interleukin-6, CRP, blood pressure, atorvastatin regimen, irbesartan regimen, duration of 
treatment, outcome measures, and adverse events. We assessed the methodological quality of 
included trials using the Cochrane risk of bias tool for RCT, which evaluated random sequence 
generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome 
assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other biases. The trials were 
grouped as low risk, unclear or high risk bias according to the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic 
Reviews. Disagreements between two reviewers were resolved by consensus. 
2.4. Statistical analysis 
Pooled effect sizes were summarized as weighted mean difference (WMD) or standard 
mean difference (SMD) with its 95% confidence intervals (CI) for continuous data. Dichotomous 
data were pooled as the risk ratio (RR) with 95% CI. The Chi-square test and Cochrane Q statistic 
were used for assessment of heterogeneity. Significant heterogeneity was defined as the I2 value 
≥50% and the Cochrane’s Q statistic p<0.10. A random effects model was selected when 
significant heterogeneity was identified. Otherwise, a fixed-effect model was used.  
To check the possible publication bias, Begg’s test and Egger’s test were scheduled if more 
than 10 trials analyzed the individual outcomes. For the primary endpoint reported in more than 10 
trials, subgroup analysis was conducted by the dosage of atorvastatin and length of treatment. All 
the analyses were carried out using STATA 12.0 software (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA). 
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT


 
6
A p-value <0.05 was considered significant for all outcomes. 
  
3. Results 
3.1. Search results and trial characteristics 
The flow chart of trial selection process is shown in Figure 1.Our initial literature search 
produced 240 records. After reviewing the titles and abstracts, 208 articles were removed due to 
duplicates or obvious irrelevant. A total of 32 full-text articles were retrieved for detailed 
assessment. After applying our inclusion criteria, 15 trials were further excluded with various 
reasons. Finally, 17 trials [15-23,26-33] were included in this meta-analysis.  
Table 1 shows the main characteristics of the included trials. These included trials were 
published between 2010 and 2018. All the trials were carried out in China and reported in Chinese 
journals. A total of 1,390 patients with early diabetic nephropathy were identified. Sample sizes of 
the individual trials varied from 50 to 160. The dosage of irbesartan was 150 mg/d and atorvastatin 
was administrated 10–40 mg/d. The lengths of intervention ranged from 12 weeks to 6 months. No 
significant differences were found in baseline serum level of creatinine, BUN, TC, TG, and FBG 
(Supplemental Table S1) as well as UAER. The methodological quality of the included trials is 
summarized in Supplemental Table S2. Five trials [22,29,30,33,34] reported the specific 
randomized method and the others only mentioned “random”. None of the trials described the 
information on allocation concealment, blinded method, sample sizes calculation, and 
withdrawals/dropouts.  
3.2.Urinary albumin excretion rate 
Fourteen trials [16-23,26-29,32,33] reported on the outcome of UAER.As shown in Figure 2, 
there was significant heterogeneity across trials (I2=82.7%, p<0.001). A random effect model 
meta-analysis showed a significant beneficial effect of atorvastatin plus irbesartan compared with 
irbesartan treatment in the reduction of UAER (WMD -21.22 μg/min; 95% CI -26.95 to -15.50). 
Begg’s rank correlation test (p=0.827) and Egger’s linear regression test (p=0.849) did not show 
evidence of publication bias. Subgroup analyses indicated a strong effect in the studies with high 
dose (WMD -23.04 μg/min; 95%CI -31.99 to -14.08) and more than 3 months treatment (WMD 
-24.20 μg/min; 95%CI -28.38 to -20.01). 
3.3. Serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen 
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT


 
7
Eleven trials [15,16,18-22,27-29,31,33] reported on the outcome of serum creatinine. As 
shown in Figure 3, there was no significant heterogeneity across trials (I2=12.9%, p=0.322). A 
fixed-effect model meta-analysis showed a significant beneficial effect of atorvastatin plus 
irbesartan compared with irbesartan treatment in the reduction of serum creatinine (WMD -6.46 
μmol/L; 95% CI -8.52 to -4.39). There was no evidence of publication bias according to the results 
of Begg’s test (p= 0.474) and Egger’s test (p= 0.185). Subgroup analyses indicated a strong effect 
in the studies with more than 3 months treatment (WMD -8.11 μmol/L;95%CI -11.35 to -1.42). 
Similarity, a fixed-effect model meta-analysis from 9 trials [15,16,18,19,21,22,28,29,31,33] 
demonstrated a significant reduction in the serum BUN level (WMD -0.46 mmol/L; 95%CI -0.64 
to -0.27; I2=0%, p=0.584) of atorvastatin plus irbesartan than irbesartan treatment (Figure 4). 
3.4. Serum level of total cholesterol and triglyceride 
Ten trials [15-17,19-22,27-29,32] reported data on serum TC level and nine trials 
[15-17,19,21,27-29,31,32] reported data on serum TG level. As shown in Supplemental Figure S1, 
a random effect meta-analysis demonstrated a significant reduction in serum TG (WMD -1.79 
mmol/L; 95%CI -2.34 to -1.23; I2=94.8%, p<0.001) and TC (WMD -0.93 mmol/L; 95%CI -1.20 
to -0.67; I2=95.8%, p<0.001) level of atorvastatin plus irbesartan than irbesartan treatment. 
3.5.Blood glucose and blood pressure 
Six trials [19,21,26,27,29,31] reported data on FBG level. As shown in Supplemental Figure 
S2, there were no significant differences in FBG (WMD -0.10 mmol/L; 95%CI -0.29 to 0.08; 
I2=0%, p=0.635) between two groups in a fixed effect model. As shown in Supplemental Figure 
S3, five trials [15,19,20,28,29]reported data on systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood 
pressure (DBP). A random effect meta-analysis showed a significant reduction in SBP (WMD 
-2.27 mmHg; 95%CI -4.01 to -0.53; I2=0%, p=0.973) of atorvastatin plus irbesartan compared 
with irbesartan treatment. However, there were no significant differences in DBP (WMD -1.57 
mmHg; 95%CI -3.41 to 0.21; I2=49.9%, p=0.092).  
3.6. Serum CRP and interleukin-6  
Six trials [18,20,21,23,26,30] reported data on serum CRP level and 3 trials [21,26,30] 
reported data on serum interleukin-6 level. As shown in Supplemental Figure S4, a random effect 
meta-analysis demonstrated a significant reduction in serum CRP (SMD 1.57; 95%CI -2.24 to -0.9; 
I2=92.1%, p<0.001) and interleukin-6 (SMD 1.53; 95%CI -2.29 to -0.78; I2=88.6%, p<0.001) 
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT


 
8
level of atorvastatin plus irbesartan than irbesartan treatment.    
3.7. Adverse effects 
Eight trials [15,16,19,21-23,29,33] provided the data of adverse effects. Overall, adverse 
events were mild and rare. The most common adverse effects were nausea/vomiting, dry cough, 
dizziness and hyperkalemia. As shown in Supplemental Figure S5, a fixed-effect model 
meta-analysis showed that adding atorvastatin to irbesartan was associated with an increased risk 
of nausea/vomiting (RR 3.15; 95%CI 1.18–8.38) when compared with irbesartan alone treatment. 
However, there were no significant differences in hyperkalemia (RR 0.38; 95%CI 0.09–1.60), dry 
cough (RR 0.95; 95%CI 0.14–6.59), and dizziness (RR 0.53; 95% CI 0.15–0.90) between two 
groups. 
  
4. Discussion 
This meta-analysis included a total of 17 RCTs involving 1,390 patients to investigate the 
efficacy and safety of adding atorvastatin to irbesartan in early diabetic nephropathy. The main 
findings of this meta-analysis indicated that adding atorvastatin to irbesartan had additional 
benefits in reducing urinary albumin excretion rate, serum creatinine and BUN level compared 
with irbesartan. In addition, atorvastatin plus irbesartan also significantly reduced serum level of 
TC, TG, interleukin-6, and CRP as well as systolic blood pressure. However, nausea/vomiting 
associated with co-administration of atorvastatin and irbesartan was a major concern.   
Proteinuria in diabetic patients is a typical manifestation of overt nephropathy [35]. Failure to 
attain remission of proteinuria significantly increased the risk of end-stage renal disease or death 
[36,37]. Increased proteinuria is recognized as a predictor of all-cause and cardiovascular 
mortality in diabetic patients [38,39]. Therefore, reducing proteinuria is considered to be an 
important goal of treatment in diabetic nephropathy. Our meta-analysis suggested that adding 
atorvastatin to irbesartan could reduce by 21.22 μg/min urinary albumin excretion rate compared 
with irbesartan alone. Furthermore, atorvastatin plus irbesartan treatment also exert additional 
benefits in reduction of 24-h urine protein [15,26,30]. Reduction in proteinuria may be associated 
with preservation of kidney function, suggesting some benefit of lipid lowering therapy with 
respect to kidney disease progression. However, it should be noted that not all patients who had a 
reduction in proteinuria had preserved kidney function. 
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT


 
9
The most commonly reported adverse effects related to atorvastatin in combination with 
irbesartan were nausea/vomiting. However, these adverse events were usually in mild intensity. 
Elevation of serum creatine kinase and serious adverse events were not reported in the included 
trials. Therefore, adding atorvastatin to irbesartan for up to six month treatment appeared to be 
safe. However, potential adverse effects of long-term treatment should be further monitored.  
Management of hyperglycemia, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia to improve renal 
outcomes plays an important role in patients with diabetic nephropathy. Blood pressure control is 
essential in order to prevent the development and progression of diabetic nephropathy [40]. It is 
well known that inhibition of the reninangiotensin-aldosterone system (RAS) provides 
renoprotection to patients with diabetic nephropathy. Apart from reduction in urinary albumin 
excretion, our meta-analysis indicated that atorvastatin plus irbesartan achieved additional benefits 
in reducing systolic blood pressure. Despite use of RAS blockers slow the development of diabetic 
nephropathy, they do not completely stop the progression of renal disease [41].   
Inflammation and oxidative stress play an important role in the development and progression 
of diabetic nephropathy [42]. Atorvastatin plus irbesartan could significantly decrease serum TG, 
TC, interleukin-6 and CRP level in our pooled analysis. Our findings are supported by Ceriello’s 
study that even short-term atorvastatin in combination with irbesartan treatment could 
counterbalance postprandial hyperglycemia and hypertriglyceridemia induced endothelial 
dysfunction, oxidative stress and inflammation in diabetic patients [43]. 
   Several potential limitations in this meta-analysis should be noted. First, an important concern 
was the methodological flaws of the included trials due to these selected trials had unclear risk of 
bias. Second, the course of the intervention period (up to 6 months) may be not long enough to 
evaluate the progression of diabetic nephropathy. Third, significant degree of statistical 
heterogeneity was found in some continuous outcomes. The possible explanation for the 
heterogeneity may be correlated with different treatment duration and dosage of atorvastatin use. 
Finally, the current meta-analysis only included the articles from Chinese-language journals and 
potential publication bias in the trials might have influenced the pooling results. 
  
5. Conclusion 
This meta-analysis suggests that adding atorvastatin to irbesartan had additional benefits in 
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT


 
10
reducing urinary albumin excretion rate and improving renal function in early diabetic 
nephropathy patients. Given the methodological flaws of these included trials, robust conclusion 
cannot be reached. Future high-quality trials are necessary to confirm these findings and to assess 
the long-term prognosis in diabetic nephropathy. There is still an unmet need for further therapy 
and drug development to halt the progression of diabetic kidney disease.
